newsitem.title: GERMANY: German "imported inflation" risk seen limited.
newsitem.headline: German "imported inflation" risk seen limited.

text.p: A steady decline in the mark led to a worrying jump in German import prices on Tuesday, but economists say a pair of state consumer price reports indicate that price pressures here will remain tame.

Economists said in view of the price reports, they remain convinced that inflation will remain within the central bank's goal of two percent or lower, even if it does tick up slightly from last year's 1.5 percent average.

"The overall price picture remains very moderate," said Guenter Redeker, economist at Chase Investment in London. "What we see here is that weak domestic demand makes it difficult for corporations to pass on price hikes. We see that continuing for the time being."
The biggest surprise of the day came when the Federal Statitics Office said import prices here climbed 2.6 percent from a year ago in January, the strongest rise since May 1991.
The report, which was higher than expected, threatened to spark worries that a long-time German economic threat, "imported inflation," was about to take off.

The statistics office said the climb in import prices was due to the stronger dollar and higher oil prices. A strong U.S. currency raises inflation here because it costs more marks to buy goods denominated in dollars.
"In this context it should be noted that the exchange rate of the dollar against the mark was 9.8 percent higher than a year ago," the statistics office said in a statement.
Excluding petroleum products, meanwhile, import prices were up 0.6 percent from a year ago.
"Import prices were stronger than expected," said Lothar Hessler, economist at Trinkaus & Burkhardt. "Import prices will remain clearly above consumer price inflation, and that is a negative factor."
Worrying though the import prices may be, Hessler and others said they expected overall consumer price inflation here to remain tame and that the Bundesbank still has room to cut interest rates.

Two of the four west German states that make up the preliminary inflation report here reported consumer price growth for February near market expectations, easing any worries that the earlier import price data may have touched off.

The state of Hesse reported a 0.3 percent rise from the month before and 1.5 percent year-on-year while the state of Baden-Wuerttemberg said CPI there rose 0.4 percent from January and 1.7 percent from February 1996.
"I would say they were satisfying," said Ulrich Beckmann, economist at Deutsche Bank Research. "It (the CPI) was very much as expected."
Economists said that weak domestic economic growth and 4.7 million unemployed mean that companies have little room to pass on higher prices to customers.
Moreover, a breakdown of the two states' CPI data revealed that food prices are moderating after surging last month because of cold weather and that heating oil and fuel prices are under control.

The market's confidence in the inflation report was clearly demonstrated by a 17 basis point climb in the March Bund futures contract to 103.38 on a day when many had expected technical factors to drag the market lower.

"The chances are good that consumer price inflation won't climb over two percent in the coming months," said Armin Kayser, economist at Swiss Bank Corp. "But we may get close to two percent by the end of the year."
